**Twelve-tone technique**
The method of composition Schoenberg developed in the early 1920s. All twelve notes of the chromatic scale are arranged in a fixed order called a tone row, and in its strictest form no note is repeated before the others have sounded. The row and its transformations (inversion, retrograde, and transposition) then generate the whole piece. It is the foundation of serialism.

**Pierrot Lunaire**
Schoenberg's 1912 setting of 21 poems by Albert Giraud (in German translation) about Pierrot, a moonstruck commedia dell'arte clown. A soprano performs it in Sprechstimme, accompanied by a small ensemble of flute, clarinet, violin, cello, and piano. It opens with "Mondestrunken" ("Moondrunk"), and in later songs Pierrot longs for his home of Bergamo.

**Verklärte Nacht (Transfigured Night)**
Schoenberg's 1899 string sextet in D minor, based on a poem by Richard Dehmel. While walking through a moonlit forest, a woman confesses to her lover that she is pregnant by another man, and he forgives her. A concert society rejected it at first because it contains an "inverted ninth" chord that was not allowed by the rules of the time. Anthony Tudor later used it for his ballet Pillar of Fire.

**Sprechstimme**
A half-sung, half-spoken vocal style in which the performer touches the written pitches but then slides away from them as in speech. Schoenberg used it in Pierrot Lunaire and for the narrator in Gurre-Lieder, and his student Alban Berg used it in the operas Wozzeck and Lulu.

**A Survivor from Warsaw**
A short 1947 cantata for narrator, male chorus, and orchestra. The narrator, who says he "cannot remember everything," describes Jews being rounded up in the Warsaw ghetto while a German sergeant shouts at them to count off faster. It ends with the male chorus singing the Jewish prayer Shema Yisrael, which includes Deuteronomy 6:7.

**Second Viennese School**
The group of composers in Vienna led by Schoenberg, including his students Alban Berg and Anton Webern. They pioneered atonality and twelve-tone music. Alexander von Zemlinsky, Schoenberg's own teacher and later his brother-in-law, conducted the premiere of Erwartung.

**Five Pieces for Orchestra and the "Farben" chord**
A 1909 orchestral set whose movements include "Farben" ("Colors," also called "Summer Morning by a Lake"), "Peripetie," and "Das obligate Rezitativ." "Farben" slowly shifts one soft chord (C–G-sharp–B–E–A) among different instruments. This is the best-known example of Klangfarbenmelodie ("tone-color melody"), in which the changing instrumental color acts like a melody.

**Gurre-Lieder**
A huge late-Romantic cantata for soloists, choruses, and orchestra on poems by Jens Peter Jacobsen. It tells of King Waldemar's love for Tove, her murder, and his grief. In the "Song of the Wood Dove" a dove reports Tove's death, and later the cursed Waldemar leads a wild hunt of his dead vassals. A narrator speaks part of it in a style close to Sprechstimme.

**Chamber Symphony No. 1**
Schoenberg's Opus 9, a single-movement work in E major for 15 solo instruments. Its themes are built from stacked fourths. It was on the program of the riotous 1913 "Skandalkonzert."

**Skandalkonzert**
A 1913 Vienna concert conducted by Schoenberg that included his Chamber Symphony and music by Webern, Berg, Zemlinsky, and Mahler. Riots broke out during Berg's Altenberg Lieder and the concert had to be stopped.

**Moses und Aron**
Schoenberg's unfinished twelve-tone opera about Moses, who can only speak, and his brother Aaron, who sings. Fearing the number 13, Schoenberg dropped a letter from "Aaron" so that the title would not have thirteen letters. All of the opera is built from a single tone row.

**Erwartung**
Schoenberg's one-act atonal "monodrama" for a single soprano, who plays a woman searching a dark forest at night and finding her lover's dead body. It is often paired on a double bill with Bartók's Duke Bluebeard's Castle.

**Society for Private Musical Performances**
An organization Schoenberg founded in Vienna in 1918 to give carefully rehearsed performances of new music, with critics excluded. It performed reduced chamber arrangements of large works, including those of his friend Gustav Mahler.

**The Book of the Hanging Gardens**
Schoenberg's atonal song cycle for voice and piano setting poems by Stefan George, among the first works to abandon tonality completely.

**Jacob's Ladder**
An oratorio that Schoenberg left unfinished at his death in 1951, along with Moses und Aron and the Modern Psalms. It builds much of its material from six-note groups (hexachords) and is an important step toward his twelve-tone method.
